title: Which Powers of ω Are Primitive n-th Roots of Unity, and the Totient Count

problemStatement.formal: For \omega = \cos(2\pi/n) + i\sin(2\pi/n) and 0 \le k < n, \omega^k is a primitive n-th root of unity \iff \gcd(k,n) = 1; consequently \#\{\, k \in \{0,\dots,n-1\} : \omega^k \text{ primitive} \,\} = \varphi(n), where \varphi is Euler's totient function.
problemStatement.plain: The parent gallery proof shows \omega = \cos(2\pi/n) + i\sin(2\pi/n) is a primitive n-th root of unity, so its powers \omega^0,\dots,\omega^{n-1} cover all n solutions of z^n = 1. But only some of those powers are themselves generators: \omega^k is primitive exactly when k is coprime to n. This problem asks us to prove that criterion and derive the corollary that the number of primitive n-th roots of unity equals \varphi(n), Euler's totient.
whyMatters: The totient count \varphi(n) is the degree of the n-th cyclotomic polynomial \Phi_n, making this the combinatorial backbone of cyclotomy and Gauss's constructibility criterion for regular polygons.
It bridges the parent entry's analytic result ('\omega generates the roots of unity') to the arithmetic structure of the cyclic group \mu_n and the theory of primitive roots modulo n.
It yields a self-contained geometric proof of a totient identity purely from De Moivre's formula, tightening the link between complex analysis and number theory.

open: Package the coprimality criterion 'IsPrimitiveRoot ((omega n)^k) n iff Nat.Coprime k n' specifically for the trigonometric generator \omega, reusing omega_isPrimitiveRoot from the parent proof.
Derive the totient count \#\{k < n : \omega^k \text{ primitive}\} = \varphi(n) as a formalized corollary tied to \omega.
